Zoom In and Zoom In Again: Fractals and a Life Transformed from Glory to Glory
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit. (2 Corinthians 3:18)
Brothers and sisters, let me start with a quiz question. It's very simple: how long is the coastline of Britain?
You might say, "Pastor, you can look that up online in a second." But the answer is surprising: it depends on the length of your ruler.

If you use a ruler 100 kilometers long and measure section by section, you'll skip over many bays, and you'll get a shorter length. Switch to a 1-kilometer ruler, and you can take in more of the twists and turns, so the length grows. Switch to a 1-meter ruler, and you count even the bumps of the rocks, so the length grows longer still.
The shorter the ruler, the longer the coastline! That sounds absurd, doesn't it?

In 1967, the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published an article in the journal Science titled "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" With this seemingly simple question, he opened up a whole new kind of geometry. Today, let's look at this geometry together, and at God's work in our lives.
How precious to me are your thoughts, God! How vast is their sum! If I would count them, they are more in number than the sand. When I wake up, I am still with you. (Psalm 139:17–18)
1. What Is a Fractal? The Part Looks Like the Whole
Mandelbrot later gave these shapes a name: "fractals." The defining feature of a fractal is "self-similarity," which means that if you zoom in on a small part of it, it looks much like the whole.

It's a bit like Russian nesting dolls: open one, and there's another identical one inside; open that, and there's another. Only fractals are even more amazing, because every corner of them hides dolls like this.

Take coastlines first. Mandelbrot estimated the fractal dimension of Britain's west coast at about 1.25. What does that mean? A line is one-dimensional, a plane is two-dimensional, and a winding coastline falls somewhere between a line and a plane, so it's 1.25-dimensional. It's more "crowded" than a line, yet it doesn't fill a whole patch of the plane.

Next, ferns. A fern frond is made of many smaller leaflets, and each leaflet looks like a miniature fern frond. The mathematician Michael Barnsley could draw a very lifelike fern on a computer using just four simple transformation rules.

Then there's Romanesco cauliflower. The next time you see one at the market, look closely: every little spire is made of even smaller spires arranged in spirals. It's practically a math lesson growing in the vegetable garden.

What is a fractal like? It's like a great tree. The trunk splits into large branches, the large branches into smaller ones, and the smaller ones into twigs. The same branching pattern repeats at every size. So whether you look at a tree from a distance or step close to look at one branch, you see the same pattern.
The most famous example of a fractal is the Mandelbrot set. Where does it come from? Just one rule: z becomes z squared plus c, and you calculate it over and over, again and again.

That one simple rule produces an infinitely complex shape. Zoom in ten times, and new patterns appear; zoom in a hundred times, and more new patterns appear; however far you zoom in, you can never see it all.

In 1998, the Japanese mathematician Mitsuhiro Shishikura proved something astonishing: although the boundary of the Mandelbrot set is a "line," its Hausdorff dimension equals 2. In other words, this line is so crumpled that it almost fills the entire plane.

But we also need to be clear: fractals in nature are self-similar only within a certain range and stop at some level of magnification. A tree stops branching once it reaches its finest twigs; only mathematical fractals can be zoomed in on forever.

A 2021 study found that the cauliflower's fractal form comes from changes in the gene network that controls flowering: places that were meant to become flowers repeatedly grow new branching points instead. This is a very recent finding, and the details are still being explored.
One simple rule produces endless beauty at every scale. That leads us to a reasonable thought: it reflects the Creator's abundant wisdom and goodness.
The psalmist says God's thoughts outnumber the sand. Fractals are like a small window God opens before our eyes, letting us glimpse his infinitely rich thoughts.

Here's something interesting. When a person paints a picture and you zoom in, all you see are brushstrokes and grains of pigment; the closer you look, the rougher it gets. But the world God made often gets more fascinating the closer you look: a leaf, a cauliflower, a stretch of coastline, magnified, becomes a whole new world. Human work can't stand up to close inspection, but God's work grows more beautiful the more closely you look.
And the psalmist says that the thoughts of this God, whose thoughts are infinitely rich, are "to me." He doesn't only pour his care into cauliflowers; he pours his care into you and me.
3. The Same Pattern in Great and Small
Fractals teach us something very important: the same pattern holds in large things and in small things.
Jesus actually taught this "fractal principle" long ago.
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. (Luke 16:10)

Who a person is in little things is who they are in big things. Someone who is impatient with a restaurant server will find it hard to be gentle at home; someone who is careless with small accounts will find it hard to be reliable in big matters. On the other hand, someone who is willing to wash the dishes properly, answer messages clearly and show up on time has a character that, like a fractal, looks the same at any magnification.
The Image of Christ Reproduced at Every Level

God's work in us is like this too. He doesn't change just one corner of our lives; he wants the same image of Christ to be reproduced again and again at every level of our lives: at church, at home, at work, in our thoughts and intentions, even in a glance or a single word.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit. (2 Corinthians 3:18)
"From glory to glory": just like zooming in on a fractal, at every level we discover new beauty. It's an ongoing process, not something finished in a day.
Maybe you feel discouraged: "I've been a believer for so many years. Why am I still the same?" Please don't lose heart; God is still at work.

Think about that great tree. When the seed first sprouts, it's just one tiny stem, and you can't tell what it will grow into. But its branching pattern was written inside it from the start. Year after year, following the same pattern, it grows layer upon layer of branches, until at last it becomes a great tree where the birds can nest.

The pattern of Christ in your life is like that. Today it may be just a tiny stem, but as long as you keep beholding the Lord's glory and keep drawing near to him, that pattern will grow out layer by layer. Not by your own striving, but "even as from the Lord, the Spirit."
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. (Philippians 1:6)
Stepping from fractals into daily life, I'd like to share three 321 principles.

First, selflessness, the self-emptied life. Paul said, "it is no longer I that live, but Christ living in me." Selflessness doesn't mean destroying yourself; it means letting the pattern of Christ be reproduced at every level of my life, from the great direction of my life down to the tone of a single sentence.

Second, 920, the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit of the Spirit often grows from the smallest things. One act of patience, one gentle word, one decision to forgive: these are the fractals of character. The fruit you bear in small things today, magnified, is what your whole life will look like.

Third, multiplication. Spiritual life reproduces like a fractal: I follow Christ, then lead others to follow Christ, and they in turn lead someone else. The same pattern is reproduced generation after generation. This is exactly how we build God's kingdom system: not by one person doing something huge, but by each person passing on the pattern of Christ.
This week's action: choose one of the smallest everyday tasks, such as being on time, clearing the dishes or replying to messages, and do it faithfully and well as an offering to the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, today is also the last stop in our Mathematics Hall. All along the way, from why math works, Fibonacci spirals, the beauty of symmetry, the most beautiful equation, infinity and simple laws to primes and today's fractals, we have seen one thing: the universe is written in God's language.
May every calculation and every moment of wonder become worship, and may you share the glory you have seen with the people around you.

When you get home, find a leaf, a twig or a head of cauliflower, and look closely at how it branches. Look from the large to the small, then from the small back to the large. Then quietly reflect: In the smallest things of my life (a word, a glance, a habit), do I also reflect the pattern of Christ?

Lord Jesus, reproduce your pattern at every level of my life: at home, at work, and in my thoughts and intentions. Make me faithful in the smallest things, and transform me from glory to glory, to be more like you. Use me to pass your pattern on to the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
